title: heapq — heappush, heappop, nlargest
signature: heappush(heap, item) | heappop(heap) -> item | nlargest(n, iterable, key=None)
summary: Maintain a min-heap inside a plain list: cheapest-first access in O(log n), and top-k in O(n log k).
description: There is no heap *type* — `heapq` maintains an invariant inside a list you own. Only index 0 is guaranteed to be the smallest; the rest is a shape, not an order, so printing a heap looks scrambled and is correct.

parameters.name: heap
parameters.description: A list maintained in heap order. Use heapify() on an existing list.

parameters.name: item
parameters.description: Comparable item, often a (priority, tiebreak, payload) tuple.

returns: heappush returns None; heappop returns the smallest item.

examples.title: Smallest first
examples.code:
import heapq
h = [5, 1, 3]
heapq.heapify(h)
heapq.heappush(h, 2)
print(heapq.heappop(h), heapq.heappop(h))

examples.title: Priorities with a payload
examples.code:
import heapq
tasks = []
for i, (pri, name) in enumerate([(3, 'email'), (1, 'alert')]):
    heapq.heappush(tasks, (pri, i, name))
print(heapq.heappop(tasks))

examples.title: A max-heap by negating
examples.code:
import heapq
h = []
for n in (5, 9, 1):
    heapq.heappush(h, -n)
print(-heapq.heappop(h))

real_world_usage: Priority task queues, merging sorted files without loading them, Dijkstra's algorithm, and 'top ten of a million' leaderboards.

common_mistakes.mistake: Printing a heap and expecting sorted output
common_mistakes.fix: Only h[0] is the minimum. heappop repeatedly for full order.
heapq is min-only. Negate numbers, or use nlargest.

common_mistakes.mistake: Pushing tuples whose payload gets compared on a tie
common_mistakes.fix: Two equal priorities make Python compare the payload, which raises for dicts. Add a monotonic counter as the second element.

common_mistakes.mistake: Sorting a list you are using as a heap
common_mistakes.fix: Sorted order is a valid heap, but any other manual mutation breaks the invariant silently.

performance_notes: heapify O(n); push and pop O(log n); reading the minimum O(1). nlargest/nsmallest are O(n log k) — much better than a full sort when k is small, and worse when k approaches n, where you should just sort.
security_notes: If untrusted input controls priorities, it controls execution order. Bound the queue size: an unbounded priority queue is a memory vector.
